lead: Thevenin's and Norton's theorems replace a whole linear two-terminal network by one source and one resistance. The load then sees the same voltage and current as with the full circuit. This matters because a load often changes while the rest of the circuit stays fixed: a new fan, a different sensor, another stage of an amplifier. Compute the equivalent once, then get the new load current in one division. The same idea turns a complicated circuit into a source transformation and makes cascaded stages easy to analyse.
prereq: You need: Chapters 1.4, 1.6 and 1.7 for reduction, equation solving and adding source responses.

sections.h3: Thevenin equivalent: open circuit, then look back

blocks.text: A linear two-terminal network has any number of resistors and independent or dependent sources. Linear means every element obeys superposition with fixed values. Thevenin's theorem says the whole network, seen from terminals A and B, can be replaced by one voltage source V<sub>th</sub> in series with one resistance R<sub>th</sub>. The load across A and B then sees the same voltage and current as before.

items: Remove the load R<sub>L</sub> from A and B. Leave the terminals open.
Find the open-circuit voltage V<sub>oc</sub> across A and B. This is V<sub>th</sub>. Choose A positive if V<sub>oc</sub> is higher at A.
Kill every independent source: a voltage source becomes a short of 0 V; a current source becomes an open of 0 A. Keep dependent sources.
Find the resistance R<sub>th</sub> looking into A and B with the independent sources killed.
Replace the network by V<sub>th</sub> in series with R<sub>th</sub>, then reconnect the load.

blocks.where: I<sub>L</sub> is the load current in amperes; V<sub>th</sub> is the open-circuit terminal voltage in volts; R<sub>th</sub> is the equivalent resistance in ohms; R<sub>L</sub> is the load resistance in ohms.

blocks.text: The open-circuit voltage is measured with no load. R<sub>th</sub> is the resistance seen from the terminals, not the resistance of the whole original circuit including the load.

Norton's theorem is the same statement in current form. Replace the network by a current source IN in parallel with a resistance RN. RN equals Rth. IN is the short-circuit current from A to B when the load is replaced by a wire. The two equivalents are source transformations of each other, as in Chapter 1.5.

blocks.where: I<sub>N</sub> is the Norton current in amperes, the short-circuit current from A to B; V<sub>th</sub> and R<sub>th</sub> are the Thevenin voltage and resistance; R<sub>N</sub> is the Norton resistance in ohms.

blocks.text: To find I<sub>N</sub> directly, short A to B and solve the circuit. The short carries I<sub>N</sub>. If V<sub>th</sub> and R<sub>th</sub> are already known, use I<sub>N</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>/R<sub>th</sub>. Then the load current from the Norton equivalent is found by current division between R<sub>N</sub> and R<sub>L</sub>.

With dependent sources, R<sub>th</sub> cannot be found by killing all sources and reducing resistors alone. Kill only independent sources, apply a test source across A and B, and measure the other quantity. Use R<sub>th</sub> = V<sub>test</sub>/I<sub>test</sub>, keeping signs. A 1 V test source or a 1 A test source is convenient.

items: Apply V<sub>test</sub>, measure I<sub>test</sub>, then R<sub>th</sub> = V<sub>test</sub>/I<sub>test</sub>.
Apply I<sub>test</sub>, measure V<sub>test</sub>, then R<sub>th</sub> = V<sub>test</sub>/I<sub>test</sub>.
Dependent sources stay active; only independent sources are killed.

sections.h3: Load line, limits and two related theorems

blocks.text: The Thevenin equivalent gives the load line V = V<sub>th</sub> − I R<sub>th</sub>. The load fixes its own relation between V and I, such as V = I R<sub>L</sub> for a resistor. The intersection is the operating point. Change R<sub>L</sub> and only the load characteristic changes; the load line V = V<sub>th</sub> − I R<sub>th</sub> and hence V<sub>th</sub> and R<sub>th</sub> stay fixed. The new operating point is where the new load characteristic cuts the same load line.

The equivalent is valid at the terminals for a linear network. The load itself may be nonlinear, such as a diode, because the theorem replaces only the linear network behind the terminals. The equivalent does not give internal currents or internal power; it gives only terminal behaviour.

Some syllabi add the reciprocity theorem here. In a linear bilateral network, a voltage source in branch 1 producing current in branch 2 gives the same current in branch 1 when the source is moved to branch 2. Tellegen's theorem says the sum of v<sub>k</sub>i<sub>k</sub> over all branches is zero at any instant for any network obeying KCL and KVL. Only a few universities teach these in this slot.

blocks.where: v<sub>k</sub> and i<sub>k</sub> are the voltage and current of branch k, with each current entering the positive terminal; the sum runs over every branch.

figure.caption: The linear network is reduced to a 4 V source with a 2 Ω series resistance. With a 2 Ω load the current is 1 A, as the worked example computes.

spec.title: Thevenin view of a network
spec.aria: A linear network is replaced by a 4 V source in series with 2 Ω, which then drives a 2 Ω load carrying 1 A.

examples.question: A 3 Ω resistor is connected across terminals A and B and is fed from a 12 V source through 6 Ω, with the 3 Ω itself forming the shunt to B. Find the Thevenin and Norton equivalents seen by a load across A and B, then find the load current for a 2 Ω load.
steps: Remove the load across A and B. The circuit is a 12 V source through 6 Ω to A, then 3 Ω from A to B.
The open-circuit voltage is the voltage across the 3 Ω resistor. By voltage division, V<sub>th</sub> = 12 × 3/(6 + 3) = 12 × 3/9 = 4 V. Terminal A is positive with respect to B.
Kill the 12 V source: replace it by a short. Looking into A and B, the 6 Ω and 3 Ω resistors are in parallel. R<sub>th</sub> = 6 ∥ 3 = (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 18/9 = 2 Ω.

Short A to B to find the Norton current. The 3 Ω resistor is bypassed, so the source current is 12/6 = 2 A. Thus I<sub>N</sub> = 2 A from A to B through the short. Check: I<sub>N</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>/R<sub>th</sub> = 4/2 = 2 A.
The Norton resistance is R<sub>N</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> = 2 Ω, in parallel with I<sub>N</sub> = 2 A.
Connect R<sub>L</sub> = 2 Ω to the Thevenin equivalent. I<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>) = 4/(2 + 2) = 1 A. Load voltage = 1 × 2 = 2 V.
Check with Norton: current division gives I<sub>L</sub> = 2 × 2/(2 + 2) = 1 A.
examples.answer: V<sub>th</sub> = 4 V, R<sub>th</sub> = 2 Ω, I<sub>N</sub> = 2 A in parallel with R<sub>N</sub> = 2 Ω, and the 2 Ω load current is I<sub>L</sub> = 1 A.
examples.check:
V = 12
R1 = 6
R2 = 3
RL = 2
Vth = V * R2 / (R1 + R2)
Rth = R1 * R2 / (R1 + R2)
IN = Vth / Rth
IL = Vth / (Rth + RL)
print(Vth)
print(Rth)
print(IN)
print(IL)

traps: Including the load resistor inside R<sub>th</sub>. Remove the load first; R<sub>th</sub> is seen looking into the open terminals.
Killing a source the wrong way: a voltage source becomes a short of 0 V, a current source becomes an open of 0 A.
Using V<sub>th</sub> as the original supply voltage. V<sub>th</sub> is the open-circuit terminal voltage after the load is removed, not the 12 V source in the example.

Finding R<sub>th</sub> with a dependent source by killing all sources and reducing resistors. Dependent sources stay alive; apply a test source and use R<sub>th</sub> = V<sub>test</sub>/I<sub>test</sub>. The examiner's favourite is exactly this dependent-source case.

quiz.q: State Thevenin's theorem for a linear two-terminal network.
quiz.a: Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced, at its terminals, by a voltage source V<sub>th</sub> in series with a resistance R<sub>th</sub>. The load voltage and current stay the same.

quiz.q: Why does a voltage source become a short and a current source become an open when finding R<sub>th</sub>?
quiz.a: A killed independent source supplies zero. Zero volts is a short; zero amperes is an open. Dependent sources are not killed.

quiz.q: A 10 V source feeds a 4 Ω resistor in series with a 6 Ω resistor to the return. A load is across the 6 Ω. Find V<sub>th</sub> and R<sub>th</sub>.
quiz.a: Remove the load. V<sub>th</sub> is the voltage across the 6 Ω: 10 × 6/(4 + 6) = 6 V. Kill the 10 V source; the 4 Ω and 6 Ω are in parallel: R<sub>th</sub> = 4 × 6/(4 + 6) = 2.4 Ω.

quiz.q: A two-terminal network has one dependent source. With all independent sources killed, a 1 V test source gives a terminal current of 0.25 A. Find R<sub>th</sub> and state the method limit.
quiz.a: R<sub>th</sub> = V<sub>test</sub>/I<sub>test</sub> = 1/0.25 = 4 Ω. The 1 V test source must be the only independent source; dependent sources remain. R<sub>th</sub> cannot be found by resistor reduction alone.

quiz.q: A Thevenin equivalent has V<sub>th</sub> = 9 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 3 Ω. Find the Norton current and resistance.
quiz.a: I<sub>N</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>/R<sub>th</sub> = 9/3 = 3 A. R<sub>N</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> = 3 Ω.

quiz.q: Why is a Thevenin equivalent useful when only the load changes?
quiz.a: V<sub>th</sub> and R<sub>th</sub> do not depend on the load. Compute them once, then use I<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>) for every new load. The original network is not solved again.

quiz.q: A student includes the load resistor while finding R<sub>th</sub>. Explain the error and the correct step.
quiz.a: If the load is left connected, the resistance measured at A and B includes R<sub>L</sub> in parallel with R<sub>th</sub>, so the value found is not R<sub>th</sub>. Remove the load, then look into the open terminals with the independent sources killed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Circuit simulators build Thevenin equivalents internally when they linearise a transistor around an operating point; the same idea appears as a small-signal model in analog design (see Unit 4, Semiconductor Devices and Analog Circuits). Battery packs and sensor bridges are specified by an open-circuit voltage and an internal resistance, which is exactly a Thevenin pair. Search for 'Thevenin equivalent dependent source test source', 'Norton equivalent circuit simulation', and 'maximum power transfer load line'.
